input: Map out a zero-waste grocery shopping routine

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Zero-waste can mean targeting packaging waste, food waste, or both — the plan looks very different depending on which the user wants to tackle.
Access to bulk stores, farmers markets, or zero-waste shops varies hugely by location and determines which tactics are actually viable.
Shopping for one person versus a family changes the scale, the types of products needed, and the complexity of the routine.
Zero-waste products and stores can cost more and take more time; knowing the user's budget and time limits shapes what is realistic.
Whether the user shops once a week, multiple times, or uses delivery affects how the routine is structured and what gear they need.
Some people want a strict near-zero system; others want gradual swaps. The ambition level determines how rigorous or flexible the plan should be.
Knowing what 'done well' means — a checklist, a habit tracker, a shopping template — determines what format the final output should take.

gold.taskTitle: Build a zero-waste grocery shopping routine
gold.taskDescription: Create a practical, repeatable grocery shopping routine that eliminates or significantly reduces packaging and food waste.

questions.title: Which waste type are you most focused on reducing?
questions.description: Is the priority packaging waste (plastic, single-use containers), food waste (spoilage, over-buying), or both equally?

questions.title: What zero-waste stores or markets are near you?
questions.description: Do you have access to bulk-bin stores, farmers markets, refill shops, or are you mainly limited to standard supermarkets?

questions.title: How many people are you grocery shopping for?
questions.description: Are you shopping just for yourself, a couple, or a larger household? This affects quantities, product types, and routine complexity.

questions.title: Is there a weekly budget limit you need to stay within?
questions.description: Zero-waste alternatives can carry a price premium. Knowing a rough budget ceiling ensures the plan stays financially realistic.

questions.title: How often and how do you currently shop for groceries?
questions.description: Do you do one big weekly trip, several smaller trips, use grocery delivery, or a mix? This shapes the structure of the routine.

questions.title: Do you want a strict system or a gradual transition?
questions.description: Are you aiming to overhaul everything at once for a near-zero result, or would you prefer a step-by-step approach that builds habits over time?

questions.title: What would a successful routine look like as a deliverable?
questions.description: Should the end result be a reusable shopping checklist, a weekly planner template, a habit tracker, a written guide, or something else?
